elements.titre: 02 · De la feuille à la base
elements.texte:
[cheerful] We collect Inès Lefebvre’s sheet.

Her review must show on every visit to the website.

So it has to be recorded in the database.

We add a reviews table: each row holds a review posted on a product.

It has five columns: ID, customer underscore ID, product underscore ID, rating and comment.

The stars on the sheet become the rating.

The text on the sheet becomes the comment.

The customer underscore ID column links the review to Inès Lefebvre’s account.

The product underscore ID column links it to the protein she tasted.

These two columns are foreign keys.

Your turn!

The website can now show her review.
elements.apres: Inès Lefebvre’s account is linked to her review by customer underscore ID.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] Inès Lefebvre’s account is linked to her review by customer underscore ID.

Click the “Delete account” button.

We delete Inès Lefebvre from the customers table.

Her review can’t keep referring to an account that no longer exists.

What should happen to this link?

elements.texte:
[cheerful] The ON DELETE rule is set on a foreign key.

It says what happens when the referenced row is deleted.

There are three options.

With RESTRICT, deleting the account is blocked as long as the review is attached to it.

With CASCADE, the account and the review are deleted together.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] With ON DELETE set null, the review is kept.

Your turn!

But its link to Inès Lefebvre’s account is removed.

Only the customer underscore ID column becomes null.

The product, the rating and the comment don’t change.

So the customer underscore ID column must allow null.

And what if you add not null to this column?

Your turn!

With not null, deleting the account is refused.

On the product page, the review is still there, with its five stars.

Your turn!

Instead of the first name, the website shows “Former customer”.

Set null changes the link in the database.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] Each foreign key can have its own rule.

Your turn!

CASCADE suits a linked row that makes no sense without the other.

Set null suits a linked row that keeps its value without the other.

RESTRICT suits a linked row to handle by hand first.

Careful: CASCADE deletes without asking for confirmation.

In the next lesson, you’ll learn to commit or cancel everything with a transaction.
